In the lavish surroundings of a luxury restaurant, Renee's life was cut brutally short by barbed wire; now, Detective Winston must unravel the tangled suspects, Claire and Isla.

Winston found himself in the bustling metropolis, drawn by a callous crime that had surprised even him. The victim, Renee, was a rising star in the music scene and her death had shocked everyone. At the top of the suspect list was Isla, a devoted groupie of what seemed to be the rival band.

As he stepped onto the stage of what had previously been the sight of the unfortunate event, Winston remembered what led him here. A music gala where Renee’s band had triumphed and Isla’s favorite, struggled. 

Winston recalled how Isla had not taken this well. She was vocal, very vocal about her displeasure. The public declaration of her resentment - just another peculiar thing about the woman. This incident especially struck Winston because in all his discussions with Isla's friends, none of them ever mentioned meeting the band members, providing more peculiarity to Isla's obsession. 

"Meeting Isla for the second time, is it?" the stage manager asked. Winston nodded. Questions about her past had prompted more questions than answers. Publically, Isla was known to be biased against Renee's culture. Subject to discrimination lawsuits filed by those she regularly chose to isolate.

Getting into the intricacies of Isla’s life had been more complicated than catching a spider in a hurricane. She never gave a straight answer about her activities in her free time, a fact that had earned her some scrutiny.

"Constant red flags with this one," Winston mused to himself. Isla had a knack for privacy. She left the room whenever she received a phone call. Never invited her friends to the band's concerts. Always arrived alone.

On the other hand, she was known for learning survival skills from online sources. Owned a private collection of survival tools at her home, where the infamous barbed wire was reportedly found. The same barbed wire, as was later confirmed, used against an intruder some months back. 

As he was leaving, Winston got a call from a local store clerk who claimed to have sold a roll of barbed wire to Isla the day before the horrific event.

“All evidence points to her,” the store clerk had said.

“Nothing is for certain yet,” Winston had firmly replied. He knew the importance to avoid jumping to conclusions, let the evidence guide the investigation. With those thoughts, he tucked away his notepad and decided to keep a closer eye on Isla. The ball game was just starting to get interesting. His aim was to do whatever it took to ensure that this case reached a fair pitch.

As Winston cruised up to the crime scene, he took a moment to appreciate the opulence of the luxury restaurant. A grand piano player in the lobby, exotic flora, and a gourmet menu, it had it all. A lady, Claire as he would come to know, was sitting outside the restaurant in her car. She was shaking, clearly upset, her eyes teary and red.

"I suppose you're Claire," Winston guessed, peering through the passenger side window. 

"Yes," she sniffed. "I work here and in that place..." she pointed feebly towards the towering construction site in the near distance. "Merely a secretary during the day, and a skilled gardener during my time off, never a scratch from the barbed wire that fences my garden." 

"Seems like you've got your hands full," Winston remarked, eyeing the construction site. "That's a lot of barbed wire over there."

"Yes..." she said, "but I'm used to handling barbed wire. We've got some fencing my garden at home too."

"I heard you have keys to all sections of this restaurant," asked Winston.

"Yes, I do," Claire nodded, "the management insists we keep everything secure, and since I work here, they trust me with the keys."

"Why were you at the restaurant today, Claire?" He asked, looking closely at the woman in front of him. 

"I usually work at the restaurant during lunch hours," Claire responded. "Today was no different."

"Strange circumstances today, though..." Winston said. "Did you know Renee was planning to file a report about some huge financial disparities at the restaurant?"

Claire squirmed a bit at his words. "I heard something about it," she mumbled. "But it's only whispers. Renee believed there was a thief... that there was someone embezzling money from the restaurant."

"And she thought that person was you, didn't she?" Winston questioned.

Claire's face turned whiter than it already was. "I...I..." was all she could choke out. 

"She had evidence, Claire," Winston continued, taking the report out of his bag. "She'd traced back all the missing funds to your bank account." He waived it in the air between them. "She was about to expose you, wasn't she?"

"Yes," she whispered, almost inaudibly, confirming her role in the embezzlement.

Winston left Claire in her car, lost in her thoughts. Puzzles to piece together, he thought to himself, getting in his car and heading back to the precinct.

When Wilhelmina is mysteriously slain by a crossbow in her own kitchen, Detective Winston steps in to question the two primary suspects, Isabelle and Nicole, in this chilling murder mystery.

Detective Winston's smoke-filled office was filled with tangible tension as he poured over the curious case of Wilhelmina. The facts at hand seemed to spin an intricate web, but the threads only made sense one at a time. 

Nicole, art collector by profession, was ostensibly the last one to see Wilhelmina. They had been scheduled for a meeting at Nicole's house where Nicole had stayed in all day, in the very kitchen where Wilhelmina had been murdered. Winston studied the eerie photographs of the scene, the brightly lit kitchen contrasted with the grim presence of a crossbow.

Shaking his head to focus, Winston remembered his visit to Nicole's home. Her exclusive medieval-themed art pieces took his breath away, as did her pride. "My treasures," she beamed, pointing grandly to a display case which held a pristine medieval crossbow.

A memory tugged at his mind, it wasn't just the crossbow she was proud of. He recalled a discussion with a bartender, the mention of Nicole's frequent appearances at medieval art auctions. What's more, Nicole had been known to read books on crossbows, and there were even whispers among her acquaintances of her crossbow-shooting practices.

And then there were the rumors, dark whispers that followed Nicole like a specter. It seemed that almost everyone Nicole had been friendly with had died under mysterious circumstances, the very circumstances that were all too familiar to Winston as he studied the police records. 

Too many puzzle pieces, yet somehow connected. Even the seemingly mundane receipt Winston held in his hand felt like a silent hint. Nicole had gone grocery shopping recently and had the forethought to buy the deceased's favorite snacks, her groceries for the day when she'd stayed home, and which now lay untouched on the granite counter.

Winston felt the connection, not clear, yet humming under the surface. What were all these interesting coincidences? Was it pure chance that Nicole collected pieces of art connected to people who lay dead? Or that Wilhelmina, a renowned collector of medieval artifacts including crossbows, was found by a crossbow in her friend's kitchen, a friend who had somehow acquired an authentic crossbow as part of her art collection and stayed home all day?

He picked up the phone, ordered more coffee, and resumed his investigations. An intricate puzzle indeed.

Winston frowned at the laptop screen in front of him, then squinted. A plethora of eBooks on archery and yoga were being sent to Isabelle's inbox, indicating Isabelle received her reading materials digitally. A picture of the cheery-looking Isabelle, beaming next to a massive crossbow, was plastered all over her heavily used social media accounts. The caption boasted of her skills, "So proud to be part of the city archery club." He navigated to a different tab, confirming her membership of an online archery club that used crossbows.

As he studied her profile, he noted some details in her bio that surprised him slightly. Next to the information that she was a yoga instructor, it read, "Travel junkie! Always out exploring after each teaching contract!" She had also listed her LinkedIn, which Winston opened. He grimaced as he skimmed over her numerous long-term contracts in various cities, and her preferred methods of payment were invariably digital.

Determined to get a clearer picture of Isabelle, he called her up.

“Isabelle, this is Detective Winston. I’d like to ask you a few questions about the death of Wilhelmina. I’d like to meet in person,” he said.

“I’d prefer if we chat online, Detective. I’m more comfortable that way,” she replied, again indicating her strong preference for online communication.

Hours later, on a video call, Isabelle appeared composed but slightly guarded. 

"Routine is central to my yoga classes, Detective," Isabelle said, and she further explained that her yoga schedule ran like clockwork. The sessions followed a rigid timeslot and it just so happened that the fateful class in Wilhelmina's kitchen took place right around the time of the murder.

"Wilhelmina was a regular attendee in my classes, and she even offered her kitchen for one of our sessions. She thought the atmosphere would be more inviting," Isabelle shared. She paused, seemingly unsure if she should continue. After a beat, she added, "She was a sweet lady. It's sad to think she was murdered right there..."

Her voice trailed off, and she looked the detective square in the face, "I was there, in the kitchen when it happened, but I... I didn’t do anything wrong."

"On the contrary, I just finished up a teaching contract in this city and I look forward to exploring this place more, Detective," she concluded, a half-smile playing on her lips.

After the call ended, Winston sat back in his chair, taking in the conversation. As he switched back to her social media profile, the pictures of her beaming next to her crossbow kept coming back.

A notification chimed, alerting him to a new email from the forensics lab. The report stated that a crossbow could be the murder weapon.

"Interesting," Winston muttered to himself, eyes flicking back to the beaming image of Isabelle and her crossbow on the screen.

In the eerie silence of a wrestling ring, Stuart's life was brutally ended with a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston with a chilling case and two prime suspects: Shawn and Octavia.

Winston sat on the bench outside the state penitentiary, going over the leviathan-sized stack of Octavia's prison records, flicking out the pages one by one. They depicted the daily life of a woman maintaining an intense physical regimen. She was fit, she was disciplined. A disciplined, successful wrestler.

The sun faded into the horizon as he stared at the record of the wrestling event Octavia had been part of and for which she had been granted a day-release pass. The sign-off from the warden stood out even in the dimming twilight. In Winston's years of experience, it was a rare thing for a prisoner to be given such a privilege, but to wrestle? That was unheard of.

Octavia, however, was an exception. She reportedly kept up her wrestling training in prison, rigorously keeping in shape. This explained her winning streak in the prison's wrestling records. But it didn't explain everything.

A chill wind swept through the yard and Winston flipped a page, his eyes catching on a note about Octavia's disciplinary actions. Several infractions, including her use of illegal foreign objects in wrestling matches, her attacks on other inmates – even using a tray as a weapon once – were duly noted.

It was the mention of her being caught as she attempted to steal from the prison’s medical ward though, that drew Winston's attention back. This was a woman fighting, desperate even, against the grips of drug addiction. Withdrawal symptoms were known to be brutal, but rarely did prisoners resort to such extreme measures.

Moving next to Stuart's file, it was clear his troubles began long before his death. Notorious from his time smuggling drugs, he later succumbed to the law's pressure and put a stop to his operations. It was a known fact he later became a regular at wrestling events, noticing Octavia there more than once. A rehabilitation, or an escape, who could tell?

Whether his love for wrestling drew him into proximity with Octavia, or his previous life of drug-running played a part, was unclear. But while drug addiction had inflamed Octavia’s desire for the substances Stuart had dealt in his past, she too shared a passion for the wrestling spectacles for which he was known. Their paths certainly crossed more than once on wrestling's squared circle.

As Winston compiled his notes, having immersed himself in the life histories of both Stuart and Octavia, he felt a strange connection between them. The pieces were there. Now, he just had to fit them together into a telling tale of how this wrestling ring turned into a crime scene, and transformed a fit, strong woman into a suspect.

Shawn's home was an impressive sight, and the library even more so. Winston noticed it immediately upon walking in, walls nearly toppling over with books. A slight air of dust hung in the quiet, still air of the room. Some of the book spines jumped out at him - collections of works on serial killers - but he reminded himself to stay focused on his task at hand.

"Detective Winston," Shawn greeted him, rising on his entry, "Please have a seat." 

"Thank you, Shawn," Winston complied, glancing about the room. “Impressive library. Do a lot of your work in here?” 

Shawn nodded, gesturing around the room, "Yes, my sermons take a lot out of me, and preparation requires time. I often seclude myself in my study, preparing for my sermons. My faith is the core of my being, detective.” 

Winston nodded, listening to Shawn talk proudly about his devotion to his faith. He did not interrupt when Shawn spoke of his religious rituals involving lead pipes that he had been taught by elders of his faith. 

Shawn leaned back in his armchair, wiping a bead of sweat from his forehead, "In fact, detective, on the night of the incident, I was conducting a sermon for our group, right here in my home study, followed by our ritual at the wrestling field. Stuart solicited my presence to view the wrestling match and then to conduct the closing rituals."

"And how do you normally feel after these rituals? You look a bit tired, Shawn," Winston softly asked.

Shawn rubbed his eyes and sighed, "Studying and my religious work often tire me. It's a lot of late nights, yes..."

Winston nodded and stood up to leave, "I appreciate you taking the time to chat with me, Shawn. I'm sorry for your loss." 

Shawn thanked him and Winston left, noting the enclosing quiet of the study once more before he did. The library lingered in his mind, but he shut that thought away as he walked out of the house.

In the cold echo of a deserted hockey rink, Otis was found dead from a grenade explosion, and now Detective Winston must decipher the clues, suspecting Ervin and Andrew are somehow involved.

Winston let out a pensive sigh as the medical examiner rattled off the factors that spelled foul play, namely the shrapnel directly linked to a grenade. When you see something new, you remember it, he mused.

The town had been buzzing since Ervin's angry outburst in the synagogue last Sunday. Bystanders had recounted to Winston how Ervin had been shouting at a particular customer he had been consulting with, before the outburst escalated and he stormed off into the synagogue. The same customer Walter Harrison was who Ervin had consulted with before he stormed off into the synagogue, had recounted it to him with fear in his voice.

"And you say you were trembling after the confrontation, Mr. Harrison?" Winston asked after the customer finished recounting Ervin's worrying reaction.

"N-not just a confrontation," the distressed customer stammered, "Ervin, our Rabbi, he lost it – punching the walls, shouting at everyone. There’s still a visible dent where he hit."

Winston gave a slight nod, “Thank you for your cooperation,” he said before heading toward the synagogue to track down Rabbi Ervin.

Ervin Thornberg, the Rabbi, met Winston's inquiring gaze coolly. Ervin had a hardened look - the clear evidence of his military past. He was known in town as former military officer with specialized training in demolitions. Nothing could erase that part of his life.

"Quite an impressive array of memorabilia here, Rabbi," Winston remarked, scanning the room filled with various wartime relics like grenades and medals from Ervin's service days. "Your friends often tell stories of you proudly showing these off."

"Careful with those, Detective, they are from my time in the service," Ervin replied, with a hint of nostalgia creeping into his tone. "My friends, they have a way of making things sound more dramatic."

Winston was further intrigued by the hint of gossip he received from one of Ervin's neighbors, "You know, Otis had been vocal lately. He saw something he shouldn't about Ervin and the synagogue funds. Even said he was planning to go to the authorities."

With that information, Winston pitched it to Ervin, "I hear Otis saw something alarming involving you and the synagogue's funds. Heard he was seriously considering going to the authorities."

Ervin stiffened noticeably, his cool gaze flickered for a moment. "Otis talks too much," he muttered, a subtle hint of annoyance in his tone.

Just as he was about to leave, a troubling fact popped back into his mind - Otis. Otis had seen Ervin embezzling funds from the Synagogue and Ervin knew that. Winston marked it down mentally and with a brisk nod to Rabbi Ervin, made his exit. Feeling the sharp gaze of Ervin boring into his back, he needed no further confirmation.

The pieces were neatly aligning, like pieces of a puzzle, Winston could see it - But it wasn't his place to tell the story, rather gather it. So with another sigh, he slid into the driver's seat and drove off. The knot in his gut tightened as he pulled away from the synagogue - he knew his work here was far from done.

Winston pulled the collar of his jacket up and stepped into the freezing cold of the hockey rink. Alone in the rink, he squinted under the heat of the artificial light to read the deserted stands and make out the chalk lines: "Just a man and his routine...Otis was always here at this time, when no one else was present...So why Otis? Why here?"

Hours later, Winston found himself wading through the mud and foliage of a nearby hiking trail. He was there to meet Andrew, the local hiking guide, a formally trained Bomb Disposal Technician in the military, and a close friend of Otis. Andrew's hiking business had been losing traction for quite some time. His soldier-like formality was still intact, standing tall despite the fall of his flailing business, which was evident through alarming financial reports showing consistent and increasing negative balance in his accounts.

"Right this way, detective." Andrew offered, leading him through the dense woods with the authority and precision that only a man with his specialized training would possess. Andrew diligently used his army skills to ensure the safety of hikers from any potential environmental dangers on their guided tours.

"Andrew-" Winston began, striding to keep up with the trained speedwalker, "I was told you two were close. And you had asked Otis about his insurance policy recently. Care to shed some light on that?"

Andrew did not look back as he continued walking. "Sure did. Otis had been open about his routine. I always knew when he was at the rink or off somewhere else. As for his insurance, he had approached me for advice and later updated it, naming me the beneficiary."

As they neared Andrew's hiking spot, Winston noticed a military-grade tent with tools, knives, ropes, canned food supplies, and hidden among them, explosives. Andrew's intense secrecy hinted at something more - these were not just regular hiking supplies.

"Quite a collection here, Andrew. Comes in handy during your hikes I presume?" Winston asked casually. Andrew replied with a nod, "It's an efficient system. Every item serves a purpose."

Before Winston could probe further, his phone buzzed, indicating a call from the station. "Just bear with me, Andrew," Winston excused himself. Andrew shuffled uncomfortably nearby, sparked a further conversation about Otis' recent insurance update.

A forensic update from the station linked the lethal grenade to the recent military base theft!

"Do you mind if we take this conversation downtown, Andrew?" Winston turned around. Andrew stood tall, showing no signs of discomfort. He simply nodded and followed Winston, all the while maintaining his usual formal demeanor.

In the chilling silence of an abandoned hockey rink, Justin was found lifeless, strangled with a rope; Detective Winston now must dissect the truth from suspects, Yvette and Lillian.

Detective Winston looked out over the hockey rink, her breath fogging as she exhaled in the crisp cold. Justin had been such a force in his team, respected, a captain among men, though some might say too powerful. Now his power was reduced to the echo of ice skates and a somber memorial created by a grieving fan base. Justin had been planning to retire soon. The season had been hard on the team, one loss after another piling on each other, and perhaps that weighted on Justin’s mind. He spent a lot of time at this rink, long hours practicing, lamenting, dwelling.

As cold as the rink was, Winston had another colder, less inviting place to visit - Lillian, a self-proclaimed follower of hockey and a big fan of Justin's team. She'd made her way to the rink too and spent a notable amount of time on the ice when the security cameras had proven to be faulty, no eyes spying her presence. The timing of her visits struck Winston as interesting. 

Winston arrived at the therapy center where Lillian was a patient. All around her, she saw various intriguing treatments - the use of ropes for exercise prominently in use. They seemed innocuous, everyday objects one wouldn’t look twice at in this setting, yet she had to remember that one such rope was the murder weapon. The center’s policies were loose, not closely monitoring rope use or restricting patients from borrowing it.

She found Lillian in one of the therapy rooms, working through her regimen, her face a mask of exerted effort as she battled her way through a routine with the ropes.

“How are your sessions coming along, Lillian?” Winston asked. 

Lillian paused, sweat glistening off her forehead. “It’s been therapeutic, they are helping me," she replied.

Winston watched as Lillian resumed her therapy. She mused over a nugget of a conversation Lillian had with a friend she'd come across in her investigation. "I would make a better captain than Justin," Lillian had bemoaned.

Winston looked at Lillian, her determination in handling the ropes, her eyes set out on a possible future where she could fill Justin’s skates, and couldn’t help but think of how Justin’s power had irked Lillian.

Winston walked away from the center, leaving Lillian to her thoughts and her rope therapy. But as she got in her car, she couldn't shake off the eerie feeling of rustling ropes echoing in the cold air of the rink and the fierce determination in Lillian’s eyes.

Instinctively, Winston flipped open his notepad as he arrived at the local hockey rink. It was here, behind the rink, that Justin had been killed. His neighbors had mentioned an unusual quiet at his house recently, which stirred further suspicion. The place still held the cold dread one felt when faced with such an incident. He was here to talk to Yvette, the choreographer, a key witness who was present at the scene for the setup.

A quick glance around the rink spotted her immediately. Yvette, poised and expressionless, stood at a distance overlooking the rink. Her stance reflected her dedication to her work - her reputation in choreography was indeed her lifeline. But her presence at the rink during Justin's murder raised alarms in Winston's mind.

"Yvette?" Winston confirmed, striding across the rink to meet her.

"Yes, detective," she replied, her voice cool and composed.

"Busy day?" Winston casually started, looking around the place.

"Always," Yvette conceded, then added almost immediately. "I insist on having my private life, so I condense my work."

"Convenient," Winston thought aloud. "And the dance studio? Neighbors said it's often closed. Unexpectedly."

Yvette paused before responding, "My trips. I need them for my creative process."

Winston nodded, letting a silence hang for a moment. "Lot of work preparing for a show, huh?"

"Absolutely." Yvette replied with a trace of bitterness. "Justin was actually set to give his speech during intermission. I saw an early draft. It was... brutal."

Winston noticed the change in her tone. "Against you?"

Yvette nodded, adding, "Justin was planning to insinuate that my choreographies were... stolen."

"I see." Winston’s eyes never left Yvette. Recalling the neighbors' remarks about the unusual quietness at her house, he pondered on it for a moment. But in the world of murder mysteries, nothing was clear cut. "Well, I appreciate your cooperation, Yvette."

He left her standing there, on the ice. Earlier, he'd have viewed her differently, a choreographer, a creator. But facts were facts, and Yvette was found on the crime scene during Justin's murder.

In the eerie silence of the swamp, Charlie's life was claimed by a crossbow, leaving Detective Winston in a murky world of deception, suspicion and the two possible culprits: Nathaniel and Bridget.

Winston sighed, coffee in hand, as he observed Nathaniel from across the yard. Nathaniel was methodically dissecting an entire neighborhood's refuse, picking valuable items that seemed to spark his interest from the detritus he sifted through. On Nathaniel’s trash run, he had picked up a wooden stick that sharply resembled a crossbow.

“Hey Nathaniel, are you a huntsman by any chance?” Winston asked walking up to him. Nathaniel replied, “Well, yes, as a matter of fact, I am. I have a hunting license, and I even won a few archery contests back in the day.” His eyes twinkled at the memories. Winston nodded, keeping any additional comments to himself. 

On the way back from their brief conversation, Winston noted something unusual for a garbage collector: an open novel, placed neatly beside Nathaniel’s bagged lunch. A genre-specific novel no less; its contents filled with murder and mayhem. Meeting Nathaniel's gaze, he nodded towards the book and asked, "Reading on duty?" Nathaniel chuckled and said, "Aye, there's no policy against it, and the higher-ups don't seem to mind. It often makes for good conversation with coworkers. I often bring these novels to work as well. They come in handy during those discussions ironically."

Intrigued, Winston checked with some of Nathaniel’s colleagues later that day. What he found was surprising - they all confirmed Nathaniel was quite the connoisseur when it came to discussing murder plots, often using his thriller novels as references. Oddly enough, he rarely brought any other type of books, always favoring murder and mayhem it seemed.

As Winston's day wore on, he remembered a report he had seen in the precinct earlier, filed by none other than Charlie. Charlie had reported missing valuables, specifically on the days Nathaniel would have his trash collection route.

Winston also recalled a secondhand report about a public confrontation between Nathaniel and Charlie. The report stated that Charlie had "called out" Nathaniel for stealing his valuables from his trash. Piecing it together, Winston realized that Charlie's accusations and the missing items correlated with Nathaniel's collection days. He sighed, wondering if the rumors held any weight.

Remembering another piece of information he picked up earlier, he roamed to the back alley adjacent to Charlie's house. Nathaniel was indeed seen sifting through Charlie's trash on multiple occasions, acquiring items of value. This linked well with what the confrontation and the report seemed to suggest. However, none of this established Nathaniel as Charlie's killer.

As Winston drove back to the precinct, he couldn’t shake off the circular puzzle that had begun to form in his mind, a puzzle as murky and enigmatic as the swamp that held Charlie's lifeless body. But his instincts had served him well before, and he was determined to see the case through, wherever it may lead.

Having a quick glance at his notes, Winston's eyes lingered on some key details about his prime suspect in this murder case. Bridget, the ex-wife of Charlie, who was without an evident alibi for the time of the murder. Charlie's life ended tragically in the heart of the swamp, a place where he loved to visit, quite often alone. He was taken down by a lethal crossbow bolt. Recalling that Charlie had changed his will last week without telling Bridget, Winston felt a twinge of unease. He shook his head, massaging his tired temples before heading off to where Bridget was staying.

He found Bridget in her backyard, busy practicing with her crossbow—an activity she was ardently committed to, despite varied environments. Her talented handling of the weapon suggested much experience, most likely from her hunting trips to the swamp with her ex-husband, Charlie. Lying next to her crossbow was a pack of new bolts, recently purchased, Winston pieced together. 

"Bridget?" Winston asked, stepping forward. 

"That would be me," she replied, setting her crossbow down on a nearby tree stump.

"Bridget, it seems like you knew Charlie would be at the swamp the day he was killed," he pointed, maintaining eye contact whilst pulling out his notepad.

"Yeah, we used to fish and hunt out there a lot. Charlie loved that place. Why?" she asked guardedly.

Ignoring her question, he inquired again. "It says you've been defaulting on your loan repayments lately and your business declared bankruptcy recently. What else aren't you telling me, Bridget?"

Looking both surprised and annoyed, she retorted by defending herself, "I have nothing to hide."

Winston merely nodded, scribbling a few notes down before leaving Bridget in the backyard next to her fresh set of crossbow bolts. The wheels of the investigation were starting to turn and Winston intended to ride the momentum until he found Charlie's killer.

In the glitz and glamour of a bustling casino, a deadly secret unfolds as Iris is found lifeless by a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston with two puzzling suspects - Madison and Christine.

Winston struck a match, lighting his pipe and eyeing his case files splayed out on the desk before him. He had a slight headache after a long day of looking into the mysterious death of a lady called Iris. A sad story really, she was a frequent visitor at the casino, she had the luck of a devil. She often walked out of that place with a smile on her face and a hefty amount in her purse...until the night she didn't walk out at all.

Sifting through the evidence, Winston's hand found an envelope labeled 'Confidential.' Inside, there was a recorded statement Iris had given to a trusted friend a few days before her death. Iris clearly expressed her intention to report Christine at her next police visit.

The only real link he had to the case so far was Christine. Christine was a solid, muscular woman who worked long hours at a construction site. It wasn't just her construction job that kept her fit, it was also the time she spent with Iris working on a shared construction project. It was during these long hours they spent together that they built a strong association, a teamwork which often led them to the casino.

Christine, during one of their teamwork endeavors revealed to Iris her involvement in certain illicit activities. Iris, shocked by this revelation, clearly intended to report these activities to the police, a fact she expressed in the recorded statement Winston now held in his hands.

Another peculiar detail, a lead pipe -- the same type as the murder weapon -- was discovered at Christine and Iris's collective work site. Christine certainly had the brawn to wield that pipe.

Winston flipped open the file and spread out the still shots from the casino's surveillance footage. A timestamp in the corner corroborated with his notes -- Christine was present at the casino the night of the murder.

The police station was quiet as he entered Christine's holding cell. The woman looked tense but tried to put up a brave front.

"Spending a lot of time at the casino and the construction site these days?" He asked.

"Sure, ever since Iris and I started working on that project together. We often celebrated our small victories at the casino" Christine's voice choked a bit on her friend's name.

"And during those hours you told Iris about your...extra-curricular activities?" Winston pressed further. Christine didn't deny it, remained silent.

"Iris had planned to turn you in you know?" Winston said coolly, fanning out the recorded statement. "This was her intention during her upcoming visit to the police station."

Christine didn't respond, just locked her gaze onto Winston's.

"I noticed a lead pipe lying around your shared construction site, identical to the murder weapon," he pushed further. "Now, Christine, what else did you two discuss when you were working on those projects?"

Winston sat back, letting his words linger in the chill air of the interview room. The pieces of the puzzle were slowly falling into place, but the game was far from over.

Detective Winston scoured through the casino surveillance footage once again, his grim reflection faintly visible on the monitor screen. There was Madison, peering into what looked like a 'souvenir' box, a curious mix of nostalgia and uncertainty etched on their face. Not a lead, but perhaps another piece of the puzzle.

A separate clip caught Winston's eye, revealing Iris within the casino, merrily wagering lady luck amidst a sea of other gamblers. Iris and Madison under the same roof. It made sense something had transpired, but it was not his place yet to jump to conclusions.

Subsequent investigation took Winston to Madison's apartment. Reports had come in that they were often seen witnessing Iris's Friday night departures for the casino. Madison, it seemed, had an insight into Iris's late-night gambling endeavors, if only because they both shared the same neighborhood.

A new twist arrived in the form of an overheard conversation. Madison, just within earshot of Winston's position, seemed to be reminiscing about overhearing Iris's tales of the casino's allure. It didn't boost the investigation, but it added an interesting dynamic.

As the day wore on, Winston moved to the next building with a lead. Madison, seen using a key to enter the previous tenant's apartment, raised some questions. On being questioned about possessing this particular key, Madison nostalgically said, "Ah, such memories." The janitor confirmed that Madison had indeed requested a copy of the previous occupant's keys. A favor for an old friend or something more sinister?

The detective moved his inquiry to the legal hullabaloo that suddenly had Iris at the heart of it. Surveillance footage showed her in the courthouse with an armful of court documents. Iris was no ordinary casino patron but a key witness in a court case directly linked to Madison's illegal activities. This implied a new layer of complication to their association.

Legal terms printed on an eviction notice in Madison's possession stated that any illegal activities could lead to immediate eviction. Madison, having received this, was acutely aware of the implications of Iris' testimony.  A visit to the casino and the courthouse, another twist in the tale, was when Madison's lawyer had to break the news to their client about Iris's damning testimony.

But for Winston, there was still a bunch of questions left unanswered, and the jigsaw was only half complete. The investigation had to dig deeper. There was a long day ahead. Pieces were moving, and Winston knew well enough in this game; nothing moved without a reason.

This had resulted in his untimely demise.

Her social media was a cascade of her embracing scissors, needles and other sharp filaments in her ostensible designs. Objects that, considering enough technique, can be reshaped into a dangerous weapon like a shiv.

He flipped through the photos of Zara's workspace. There was a toolkit - an array of sharp, glimmering instruments specifically designed for crafting fashion. They also gave Winston a hint of a chilling familiarity with the puncture evidence.

"Tell me again," Winston asked both of them in turn, "when did you hear Zara's car start?"

"Just after her room light went off," they iterated, almost in chorus, "like clockwork."

"Floyd?" She asked. "What has happened?"

Winston said, "Our investigation revealed that he was continuously asking you for the money you owed him." He further added, “He was planning to take legal action if you didn’t pay, proof of which we found in his office."

Upon hearing this, Catherine responded, "Yes, he was putting me under a lot of pressure to pay back.” She then pointed towards her busy calendar placed on her desk and revealed, "We had a meeting scheduled today at the library to discuss the matter, it's right there in the calendar."

Confirming Floyd's attendance at the meeting Winston adds, "Yes, we've checked the library's sign-in book and confirmed that Floyd did check in for the meeting."

Catherine shrugged. "I was supposed to meet him there. About my debts to him."

"Your debts..?" Winston asked, raising an eyebrow. "Would you care to talk more about it?"

"Not much to say detective," shrugged Catherine, "I owed him money... wasn't able to pay."

"Why weren't you able to pay this debt?"

She sighed heavily with a far off gaze in her eyes as truth revealed itself. "I'd been missing a lot of mortgage payments. Had to sell my airplane. Just haven't been able to make ends meet..."

Winston shifted his gaze to a bag that sat on a nearby desk. Marked beside it were a few library books. Catherine followed Winston's gaze. "I took them from the library," she admitted. That would explain why her fingerprints were all over the books.

Winston smirked lightly. "And the librarian confirmed seeing you there, around the time of Floyd’s murder.”

Catherine nodded. "Yes, I was."

Catherine chuckled lightly. "Well, yes. And as you can see," she pointed towards her bag on her desk, wherein upon casual inspection Winston found the shiv, "I never stopped practicing. It makes me feel safe to have it with me."

The shiv perfectly fit the description of the blade used in the murder of Floyd. It was the perfect weapon for a practiced hand to use quickly and quietly in a crowded library. 

But Winston merely nodded to himself as he jotted down a note or two. "You're full of surprises, Catherine." … [잘림]

When the silver screen flickered with an unexpected explosion, claiming the life of innocent Chloe, seasoned Detective Winston stepped in to unravel the deadly scandal entwining suspects Ruby and Roscoe.

Despite the night's residue of tobacco clinging to his garment, Detective Winston took a deep inhale as he approached Ruby. He pulled out a crumpled picture of Chloe from his pocket and sighed, replaying the explosion at the movie theatre over and over in his mind, as well as the image of Jake, the man he's spotted Chloe with on numerous clandestine dates.

"Ruby," he began. His voice was low and weary. "I understand that you and Chloe had planned a sister-courtship to the movies last night."

A flicker of surprise crossed Ruby's face. "Why, yes. Chloe wanted to see that new film, The Scarlet Phoenix. We enjoyed a night at the theater till the very end. Nobody else entered or left the theater during our stay - it was just us."

"Interesting," muttered Winston. "And there were eyewitnesses confirming that you were the last person seen with Chloe?" 

"Yes," said Ruby hesitatingly,"We departed together."

"Interesting," muttered Winston, making no further comment. Instead, he considered the reported vision of Ruby seeing Chloe kissing another man. Another man who turned out to be Jake.

"I understand that you might have feelings for Jake. Is that right?" Winston questioned, watching Ruby carefully.

Ruby hesitated, playing with the locket around her neck. “Yes, I suppose that's true,” she admitted, but never meeting his gaze.

The detective changed the angle of the conversation. “I've heard tales about your psychic abilities, Ruby. You tend to see dangerous things. Your visions included dreadful bomb scenarios back when you were in the military, right?”

"I've had visions," Ruby replied defensively. "Visions are often ambiguous. They can symbolize various scenarios. I did see Chloe, Chloe kissing another man... Jake. And yes, during my service, I’ve seen how war and destruction unfold, even how to use grenades."

"I can imagine," Winston said, thinking to himself. Connecting the dots, he continued, "Did you know that Jake and Chloe were secretly seeing each other?"

Ruby's apprehension told Winston everything he needed to know. "Yes, I knew. Chloe told me about it," she said, her face growing pale.

"Did you also stay behind after the movie, in the theatre?" Winston asked, looking at Ruby sternly.

"We both enjoyed the ending credits music, so we stayed till the end. I distinctly remember walking out of the theatre last night, but... alone," Ruby said, hinting at her absence following the movie's completion.

Winston allowed a moment's pause before continuing on. "Ruby, where did you go after the movie ended?"

"I went to my brother's house," Ruby's reply was swift, a touch too swift.

Winston blinked, remembering her brother's notorious reputation as an arms dealer, and Ruby's own military background. "That's... convenient."

"I suppose it is," Ruby replied quietly, eyes fixed on the policeman's tired, yet zealous gaze. The meeting was concluded with that, leaving Winston with the chilling evening wind and another lead in Chloe's puzzling demise.

Winston glanced at the movie ticket stub Roscoe held, noting that it was for the same film as Chloe. He squinted at Roscoe, who was a respected astrophysicist and dedicated military officer, but his current disheveled appearance suggested a disconnect. 

"You were here at the theatre when the event happened, then?" Winston asked, gesturing at the ticket. Roscoe was indeed there before the movie started, now confirmed by the timing on his ticket. 

A confirmed nod came from Roscoe, who avoided meeting Winston’s gaze. "Yeah, I was here. Same movie as her." His voice dropped lower. "When the incident occurred during the movie screening. Chloe... She didn't make it."

Winston hesitated, knowing Chloe's death wasn't the only thing he needed to discuss today. Throughout their conversation, Winston noticed a limp in Roscoe's step, bruises, and a sharp wince when he moved a certain way. "Looks like you've got some injuries there," Winston remarked casually. 

Though he spoke offhandedly, Roscoe was quick to brush it off, often changing the subject when questioned about his injuries, which drew Winston’s attention. More so than before, Winston observed, people tended to notice when someone was deliberately avoiding a topic.

Trying not to push too far, Winston paused momentarily - but then he remembered the drug bag found in Roscoe’s possession at the theater. He recalled a report from resident neighbors as well, Mr. & Mrs. Davenport, stating that they've often seen Roscoe limping into his apartment late in the night, disheveled and pained. Further arousing suspicion was the doorman’s testimony, reporting a similar disheveled state during the late-night arrivals.

Remaining cognizant of the consequences to Roscoe’s military career if he were to be caught using drugs, Winston pressed on, "Roscoe, I've heard you've been behaviorally inconsistent at work lately. And there’s the matter of the confiscated drug bag. Do you understand the negative implications this could have for your military career?"

Roscoe visibly flinched. His demeanor took on a nervous edge, scratching his arm as it often did when he felt cornered. Winston’s gaze hardened, feeling certain that Roscoe was the name written in secret within Chloe's notebook. The one she intended to report for drug usage.

“I...uh got to use the restroom," Roscoe stammered before rushing off, undoubtedly the effects of the drugs kicking in.

Winston decided to follow, needing more answers. Was Roscoe the reason behind Chloe's demise? Was this why he'd jeopardize a promising military career with drug addiction? With renewed determination, Winston set off after him.

As Winston neared the restroom, he was eerily reminded of the nearly empty crime scene — a movie theatre mid-showing. He shuddered at the thought … [잘림]

In a seedy motel room, Frederick's life was cruelly punctuated with a corkscrew, leaving Detective Winston to unravel the twisted tales of two suspects, Tessa and Van.

Winston's dispatch message included the name "Tessa". He remembered her as a skilled bartender at a high-end restaurant, famed for her unique way of handling a corkscrew, especially while opening extravagant wine bottles. Recently, she seemed to have been working outside of normal working hours. She was often seen requesting financial support from Frederick, an affluent regular customer who wouldn't mind doling out his means for attention.

A friend once mentioned to him Frederick’s intention to spill the beans about Tessa's grim reality. It was not every day someone aimed to settle a debt of that size, and the situation intrigued Winston. Using the information he had, he traced that Tessa had checked in the motel a couple of days before Frederick’s demise.

Winston pulled his sedan into the dusty lot of the low-rise motel on the outskirts of town. There he saw Tessa, emerging from a room and handing a key back to the motel manager. The motel staff confirmed that the implicating room was indeed paid for by Tessa, and their logbook showed that she had checked in before Frederick’s death. They also agreed that she had remained on the premises throughout.

The day Tessa was arrested, she displayed her usual calm demeanor. As the police handcuffed her, a metallic shine of a corkscrew slipped out from her apron pocket, landing on the ground below. This was her personal corkscrew, a tool she always had on hand for her routine work at the restaurant, and one that she was seen using frequently to open wine bottles during her shift.

As Winston left the motel to return to the precinct, he mused over the victim’s connection with Tessa. Frederick knew about Tessa’s considerable debt, and this was not ordinary behavior between a server and a regular patron. But for now, the facts just laid out the circumstances. His sole contribution to this puzzle would be to compile the facts so they could make sense. The rest — the swift execution of justice — was a matter of time. And Winston knew that time always brought the truth to light.

Winston straightened his tie as he approached the scene of Frederick's murder, squinting under the motel's harsh fluorescent lighting. Frederick, a successful events planner, was stealing lucrative contracts right from Van’s territory. On the other hand, Van also managed to poach a few of Frederick's prime clients. Frederick's competitors saw his success as the rising spark of a problem they had to deal with. Someone like Van, maybe. 

Van. The one who was always behind a desk at every event he planned, for some reason avoiding any kind of physical exertion. For instance, at every event, he could be found refusing a spot in the robust, physically-demanding relay races that colleagues customarily participated in. That night was no different, the event was a wine tasting. Van would likely be there, not participating in the traditional grape-stomping competition. There, Van would flaunt his newly-acquired clients; the ones he had usurped from Frederick.

With this thought in his head, Winston drove over to the event, arriving to the sight of Van pouring wine expediently with a corkscrew for the event attendees instead of joining in on the active games. 

"Van," Winston greeted, nodding at him.

"Detective," Van replied, raising an eyebrow. 

He paused as Winston took a seat in front of him, then offered a bottle of red. "Wine, Detective?"

"No, thanks," Winston said, "Don't you usually have an assistant to open wine bottles?"

Van laughed, shrugging off the observation easily. "I like doing it. It's therapeutic," he said.

Then there was the fresh dressing peeking out from under Van's cuff, the one he offered some vague explanation for, just like every other time Winston had seen him injured. He referred to these as ‘small accidents’.

He remembered what Van's colleagues had said about him. Always getting injured, never playing in any games, always behind a desk, and there was that thing with Frederick. 

"Frederick," Winston started, both men looking somber at the mention of the recent murder. Van averted his gaze, focusing steadfastly on the bottle he was opening.

"I heard you had a falling out."

Van sighed, and for the first time that evening he looked tired. "Fred and I... we had our differences. He was snatching clients right under my nose. And I wasn't just taking it lying down, I got back at him by snatching some of his clients,” he confessed. 

"Heard you even threatened him once," Winston said quietly.

"That was just business, nothing personal," Van replied coldly. "If you're suggesting--"

Winston lifted his hands, chuckling lightly. "I'm not suggesting anything, Van," he said carefully.

Turning his attention back to the bottle, Van popped the cork and poured himself a glass. "Fine. I had my disagreements with Frederick," he admitted. "Yes, we threatened each other over clients. But that's all it was... just threats."

Winston left shortly after, leaving Van to his wine and his thoughts. As he walked back to the car, he remembered the coroner's report. Those puncture wounds in Frederick's autopsy. Consistent with a corkscrew... 

A steady cold rain fell on Winston's windshield as he drove away, leaving behind the warm lights of the wine tasting event and a man with a lot on his mind.

In a chilling turn of events, Rose is found lifeless in a car, killed by a vial of acid, leading Detective Winston to the affluent suspects, Daisy and Dexter.

Winston was going over the facts of the case when he decided to visit the suspect, Daisy. Daisy wasn't your typical suspect - she was a singer who always had a passion for her art form, a passion that stood in sharp contrast with her family's dismissive attitude.

“I'm just trying to get ahead in life, you know?" she told Winston as they sat in a small cafe near one of her repeat performance venues - an old building that was frequently harshly criticised for its lack of cleanliness. "They never cared about my music… always thought it was just a phase. I couldn't stand their lack of support.”

Getting rid of her family members from her contacts was, as she put it, a "cleansing experience". It was all very telling of Daisy's meticulous nature - she extended the same cleanliness philosophy to everything in her personal life, hygiene being her top priority; it gave a stark contrast to the venues in which she performed.

After a moment of silence, she casually added, "Sometimes my sarcasm gets the best of me. I can't tell you how many family dinners I've ruined with it. My sarcasm stings so hard, it often leaves them in tears."

Winston thought about Rose, who often parked her car in the same vicinity. "You were scheduled to perform at a place near that parking lot that day… right?" he asked. Daisy affirmed the fact and mentioned having seen Rose's car, acknowledging that she and Rose were the last two people in the vehicle after her show that night.

As part of her performances, Daisy often integrated different kinds of acid into her routines - the same kind, as it turned out, that had been used to murder Rose. A cold chill ran down Winston’s spine as he mentally cross-checked the evidence list.

“Acid isn’t a typical instrument for a singer, Daisy..." Winston quizzed, trying to keep the conversation casual. Daisy just shrugged, "Got to create a spectacle, right? Attract an audience?”

Daisy had always been adamant about not attending any family gatherings - a fact that did not change even after Rose’s death. But she claimed to hold no ill-will towards Rose. As Winston got up from the table to leave, he turned one final time to look at Daisy who was now alone and engrossed in her phone. A suspect or not, one thing was certain, the story was far from over.

Winston reeked of grease and sweat as he strolled into the electronics store, blinking against the twisted glare of neon and the sharp gleam of fluorescent lights. Dexter, a wiry man in neatly pressed slacks and a polo, paused in checking and restocking the freshly stocked batteries to greet him.

"You look lost, sir," he called, a spark in his eyes belying the monotony in his voice.

"Actually, I have a few questions for you, if that's not too much trouble," Winston started, flipping open his notepad to gather his thoughts.

A flicker of unease crossed Dexter’s face, but he masked it quickly, "Sure, always happy to help."

Winston dove straight in, "Know a woman by the name of Rose?"

Dexter's face tightened imperceptibly. "Rose, yeah. I know of her. She left her car here to get cleaned the other day. She told me that she had found an embarrassing picture of me somewhere."

"So, you work on cars too?"

"I... not exactly. I was on duty when she came by. We don't usually offer those services, but I took care of it," he replied, his gaze straying to the poster advertising their recently received new stock of batteries.

"What type of cleaning, exactly?" Winston asked, silently noting another stain on the pristine floors.

"Uh... just vacuuming, mostly. People leave all kinds of things in their cars," he concluded, avoiding Winston's steely gaze. "I found the embarrassing photo of myself in there, the one she had claimed to have found earlier."

"Must have seen a lot of interesting things."

"Yeah, you could say that." Dexter's voice wavered, a hint of bitterness creeping in.

"Were you alone while cleaning the car?"

"Yes. What's this about?" Panic fluttered in Dexter's eyes just as Winston showed him the same embarrassing photo of Dexter that was making the rounds in town - the one Rose had found.

"Oh," Dexter spoke, all hints of his usual smug demeanor nowhere in sight. "That... was circulating at the town gathering... and Rose had grabbed it and laughed at me as she shown it all around."

"Right," Winston said, making a mental note as he slipped the photo back into the folder. The laughter, Rose's cruel laughter at Dexter during that town gathering, rang in his memory. 

Dexter spoke after a pause, "I...didn't know she still had that."

"One more question," Winston started, leaving the silence to hang as Dexter looked about to collapse. "Your education...you studied Chemistry? Specialization, was it industrial acids?"

"Different types, yes," Dexter confirmed, struggling to keep composure. "Hydrochloric, Sulfuric, Nitric...so many..." His voice trailed off into a whisper as Winston closed his notepad.

"Interesting," Winston remarked, and headed for the door. The fluorescent store lights flickered as he strode out into the evening, leaving a bewildered Dexter behind in the now-quiet electronics store.

In the heart of the rainforest, Jesse meets his gruesome end by a lawnmower, leaving Detective Winston embarked on a puzzling quest with suspects - Sam and Steve.

Detective Winston stood at the edge of the rainforest, reviewing his notes. The scene was grim, even for a seasoned detective. The body of Jesse, a young boy, had been found. The murder weapon, found near his body, was a lawnmower, an odd choice for a murder weapon, especially in a rainforest.

One suspect was Jesse's fellow schoolmate, Sam. His name had surfaced around the investigation thanks to a tip-off from the school janitor. The man remembered seeing Sam at the lost and found desk, writing something.

It appears that Sam had found some incriminating texts on his girlfriend's phone, all of which were sent by Jesse. When confronted, Sam's girlfriend confessed that she had been seeing Jesse behind Sam's back. This all coincided with the fact that Sam had access to paper and pen during his visit to the lost and found desk. Winston also learned that the numbers from the confiscated phones were noted down on a piece of paper.

The field trip group Sam and Jesse were part of were the only ones in the rainforest that day. Sam was among them, having also been given special privileges, being the only student allowed to access the lost and found box. Winston made yet another note of it. 

"Winston," a fellow detective called out, causing Winston to look up. 

"What is it?" He asked, heading towards the man.

"Just wanted you to know, we've seized the phones. The numbers were written down."

"On paper?"

The detective nodded, "Yeah. At the lost and found desk, from what we've heard."

Winston's eyes squinted as he thought. He knew these facts were significant, but their connection was not clear. 

"Okay. Thanks." Giving him a nod, he moved towards his vehicle. 

His mind whirled with facts as he started the car. Conversations with Sam, his fellow schoolmate's murder, confessions from his girlfriend, and peculiar facts from a field trip in the rainforest. 

He knew his job wasn't done until he found justice for Jesse, until he was able to connect the dots and bring the story together. For now, he just needed to keep gathering facts and truths. 

Every puzzle piece counted.

Rain pattered on the windshield as detective Winston drove toward the rainforest. A call had come in, a body, Jesse's, found in the woods. As the victims' details appeared on his screen in flickering neon blue, Winston registered one significant point that had yet to be confirmed - the murder weapon was a lawnmower.

Upon arriving at the scene, he climbed out of the car, his shoes squishing and sliding in the mud. It was time to pay a visit to the prime suspect, Steve, a dedicated Rabbi trying to make ends meet.

His visit to Steve was brief but loaded with significant information. To the unsuspecting, Steve was a devout religious leader and a generous individual who devoted his time to frequent forest clean-ups, never too busy to lend a hand with his own set of lawnmowers.

"Lately, my congregation has been dwindling, " Steve confessed. "I had to set up a lawn care business to support myself and the synagogue."

While Steve rambled, Winston learned more about Jesse's aggressive approach to business. "Jesse... he had an ambitious streak. I couldn't compete," Steve admitted, "He was systematically undercutting my prices, offering ridiculous summer discounts and premium services."

This confirmed Winston's suspicion that Jesse had not only been a rival but was planning to put Steve out of business. Steve, however, was not unaware. He suspected Jesse of stealing his clientele and provided evidence to Winston. Steve's business was shrinking while Jesse's was blooming, a fact evidenced by the bitterness lurking in the Steve's voice whenever Jesse was mentioned.

Winston, maintaining a stone face, asked about Steve's activities on the day of the murder. As if on cue, Steve informed him that there was a clean-up event on that same fateful day, occurring at the exact time Jesse met his grisly end.

Officers at the scene had confirmed the unusual chains of Steve's lawnmower as the cause of death. Oddly enough, Steve owned several lawnmowers, all part of his lawn care business, and he was more than proficient in their operation.

On a night when the roar of go-karts was silenced by a nefarious deed, Detective Winston finds himself investigating the peculiar murder of Gary, slain by a rarely-seen sai with two unlikely suspects: Frederick and Jerome.

Winston furrowed his brow as he flipped through the case file. Jeremiah, the previous go-kart champion, was found dead at the very track he'd dominated for years. Gary, undefeated and the current champion, had been a massive hurdle for those competing, especially for his rival Jerome, who always seemed to take the second place.

An eyebrow-raising detail caught Winston's attention, Gary's keys to his office had been reported missing and unaccounted for.  The reports had indicated that a driving instructor by the name of Jerome was the last person to leave Gary's office the day his keys went missing. Winston had also found it strange that Jerome controlled the go-kart track's schedule.

Besides driving instruction, Jerome also seemed to indulge in a martial art form. An impressive certificate of martial arts mastery hung on the walls of his office.

Winston heard rumors of sustained tension between Gary and Jerome. Apparently, they had a history of contentious races, with Gary's supremacy hindering Jerome's chances at first place. Gary had recently accused Jerome of cheating in the last race, leading to a major dispute.

Unusually, a week before the murder, Jerome was seen purchasing multiple sai—a weapon Winston was familiar with from martial arts movies. Some top-drawer receipts from Jerome's office confirmed these purchases. Additionally, he was spotted practicing with the sai at a local gym, following his regular fight moves workout, fueling the mystery.

Jerome's passion for go-karting was immense, and as the track's driving instructor, he was deeply involved in all activities. This involvement granted him unrestricted access to most track areas, including Gary's office. 

At the track itself, Winston decided to question Jerome. He found Jerome instructing a group of novice drivers.

"Jerome?" asked Winston.

"That's me," replied Jerome, turning around. His gloves showed signs of frequent use. He appeared to be a hands-on instructor.

"You were close with Gary, I take it?" 

"He was a tough competitor, but we knew each other on the track," said Jerome.

"His dominance in every race must have been troublesome for you, especially after he accused you of cheating in the last one. The fact that his keys are missing and you were the last person to leave his office must be another troubling circumstance for you."

Jerome sighed, “It was his word against mine. But yes, it added more tension to our already strained relationship.”

Winston thanked Jerome for his time and decided to dig deeper into this mystery, leaving the sounds of roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber behind.

Detective Winston elegantly stepped out of his car, looking from side to side at the quiet go-kart track. Tire tracks were sketched over the quiet go-kart track. Despite the glaze of the late night, the sight oozed with an unexpected eeriness: the phantom-like go-karts parked neatly, the silent squeal of the rubber tires on the cement track, and the absence of the usual laughter, all seemed abnormal given the facts. It was much later for Frederick, the dock worker, who not only could be spotted at the track frequently, even into the late hours of the previous night, but had been spotted there exceptionally late on the murder day.

Conversational whispers echoed among the locals recently. Frederick, it turned out, had been confronting others about their unsolicited interactions with his beloved go-kart. The sight of his kart, now still and silent unlike its usual roar, coupled with the deafening quietness of the night ran chill down Winston's spine. He couldn't shake off the echoes of a recent dispute Frederick had here, not when his racing schedule strangely aligned perfectly with the murder time. And the off hours, serving less crowds, made it an ideal time for Frederick to get some of his responsibilities done, like inventory management and safety checks.

Winston moved towards a small office adjacent to the track. Opening the door, the room was not much larger than a closet with a couple of cabinets, a coat rack, and a table; provisions neatly stacked. Frederick's racing gear - a jacket, helmet, gloves - all graciously set aside on the coat rack, having a faint hint of diesel fuel. Walls adorned with race schedules and a surprising void on the ledge beside the window where a computer likely sat. As a dock worker, Frederick was naturally involved in inventory management and health and safety checks.

His thoughts drifted to Gary, another regular on the track. Before the silence followed by the sirens, someone had reported seeing Gary fiddling suspiciously with Frederick's kart. The circumstances seemed too cut and dried, further intensified by Frederick's off-hour routine at the track and a suspicious run-in with Gary.

"Ey, I heard the sirens earlier. Something's happened, ain't it?" A voice, bearing a question gripped with anxiety, interrupted Winston's thoughts. Turning, the detective found himself face to face with a night security guard.

"Yes, I'm afraid there's been an incident. You wouldn't have noticed anyone acting strange around Frederick's usual racing time earlier today, would you?"

"I don see clearly from the gate, but yeah, there's always something smack peculiar during that hour, " the guard answered, wiping his brow with a used handkerchief. His statement was an indirect validation of the conspicuous activities during the usual times Frederick would race.

The night, however quiet, was thick with implications, marred by the footprint of a crime at a go-kart track.

In the wake of a gruesome flamethrower murder at a local soccer field, seasoned detective Winston steps up to investigate, with suspects Sophia and Larry under his watchful eye.


Winston was staring at Savannah's campaign poster — the one with her promising smile and eyes full of assurance. Savannah, who was leading in the polls, was clearly the people's choice for the election. The upcoming political rally had been plastered about town for weeks, making it an inevitability known to all.

Winston scratched at an internal itch and trudged onto another stakeout. Larry, the man he was looking to question, was apparently active in a local survivalist group. Flipping open his notebook, Winston noted that Larry was a war veteran who had gone to significant lengths campaigning himself. Posters of Larry bearing the tagline "Whatever it takes" dotted the town too.

Winston watched as Larry scrutinized each one with such intensity that it seemed like his entire identity was tied to the outcome of this election. The survivalist meetings took place in Larry's private property, which he had converted into a fortified camp after pumping his entire fortune into his campaign.

Winston decided to pay a visit to Larry to know more about him and his involvement in the race. They met at Larry's camp, a spit-and-polish place that reflected Larry's military background. Crisp flags snapped in the wind and the entire setting was punctuated by the distinct scent of gun oil.

"Thank you for your service," Winston began, extending a handshake to Larry who returned it with an iron grip. It's well-known that war veterans like Larry are experienced with various forms of weaponry, including flamethrowers. True to this, an errant flamethrower was left out in the open at his camp, catching Winston's eye. A flame thrower, not entirely strange for a survivalist's camp, was an interesting detail, considering the bizarre circumstances of Savannah's death.

As they chatted, Winston learned that Larry and Savannah were political rivals. Larry preferred to attend every rally personally. In fact, even though they stood on opposing political platforms, Larry never missed any of Savannah's rallies.

"I respect my opponent," said Larry, his gaze distant. "It's her policies I have a problem with."

Winston wrapped up the brief visit with a polite nod. As he left Larry's camp, the veteran-turned-politician watched with a grim smile that left Winston looking back at Savannah's campaign poster with a different perspective.

Under the harsh whiteness of the police station lights, Winston eyed the smartly dressed woman with a critical gaze. Sophia, they called her. A journalist. She was a fine-boned woman, older, maybe late forties, with a reputation for relentless pursuit of stories. And not just that, she had a remarkable reputation of not lying or hiding truths, even under the most severe pressures.

"Sophia, you worked on coverage of the military exhibition last month, right?" he started, watching her eyes carefully for subtle reactions.

"Yes, I did," she said coolly. She looked him directly in the eyes, without a hint of evasion. "I am entrusted with sometimes sensitive information. I don't lie or hide truths, detective. I take my job quite seriously."

Seeing her intensity, Winston was not surprised. She was invested in her career, in truth-seeking, more than most. But her career, it seemed to Winston, was teetering on the edge. His notes said something about job stability issues.

"I heard from various sources that your job as a journalist could be at risk, Sophia."

A flicker of annoyance crossed Sophia's eyes. "Every job carries elements of risk and taking risks is crucial for growth, detective," she replied firmly.

Winston took note of that and moved on to another point. "Is it true that you managed to keep a flamethrower from the exhibition?"

A pause. Then a nod. "I did keep a flamethrower... to study it further for my report. Is that a crime?" she asked pointedly, her reputation for truthfulness evident. A defiant posture, not backing down easily, but then that's what made her good at her job, the detective reasoned.

"Well... does the name Savannah ring a bell?" Winston asked, trying not to flinch at the sudden stiffness that came over Sophia's features. "She knew you had a secret source, didn't she, Sophia?"

Again, a pause, then a pointed glance before she finally said, "Yes, she did... and she threatened to jeopardize the whole thing by revealing it publicly." The bitterness in her voice betrayed the gravity of that threat.

Just as he was about to dive into that area further, he was reminded of a peculiar bit of information he'd acquired. "Sophia, you were asked about some... scars? At a dinner party?"

Suddenly, all of Sophia's poise seemed to wither away. "If you’re referring to the dinner at the mayor's house, yes, I was asked about them," she answered evasively. Then she stood up in alarm, eyes flashing with a mix of fear, defiance and something Winston couldn't quite place.

"I think this conversation is over, detective. Thank you for your time," were her words before she exited the room hastily.

Winston sighed, shoving his hands in his pockets. The chapter with Sophia wasn't over yet. Not by a long shot. He admired her relentless pursuit of the truth, of not dodging or lying.

When Mack's life got fatally bleached out on a soccer field, it was up to Detective Winston to sift through the dark clues left by his suspects: Helen and Danielle.

Winston, his heart heavy with grim resolution, studied the photos of Mack's lifeless body on the soccer field. The murder scene was an unsavory juxtaposition of innocence - usually bustling with kids, laughter, and vibrant life, now tainted with the solemnity of demise and the faint smell of bleach lingering in the air. 

His next step was Helen, Mack's sole testamentary beneficiary it seemed, and his housekeeper - a critical point of interest.

Arriving at the soccer field, he spotted Helen from afar, scrubbing away at the stubborn grass stains with a generous amount of bleach - a daily routine in her housekeeping duties. She was an efficient worker, with knowledge on various cleaning products and supplies, which her job demanded.

His eyes became glued to a large quantity of bleach that Helen had with her. An unsettling thought crossed his mind, quickly followed by a dismissive wave. 

Winston introduced himself to Helen who was already there. Judging by her demeanor, he got an underlying sense of humiliation boiling within her, perhaps a result of being objectified at her job as a housekeeper. 

"Do you clean up after the games every time?" Winston asked, breaking the tense silence.

"Every single time. They don't clean up after themselves, so someone's got to do it," Helen said, her tone full of regrettable resignation, showing no signs of withholding information.

"So, you were here, even when the game was on?" Winston then asked, the seemingly benign query holding a latent inquiry.

“Yes, and Mr. Mack, bless his soul, stayed behind with me after everyone else had left,” Helen replied, burrowing her frown even further, eyes welling up with unseen tears. 

She continued talking away, inadvertently revealing how she's often at the rough end of some nasty backbiting, making Winston wonder if that might've fuelled her self-diminution.

"Are you Mack's housekeeper?" Winston asked, out of the blue, seemingly testing Helen's patience.

She stared at him for a solid minute before affirming she was, indeed, Mack's housekeeper. Mack, she recalled, even included Helen's role in his will, stating that she should run the house in the event of his untimely demise. 

With an interview like this, it was hard not to observe how it all seemed to add up, but Winston prudently kept his findings to himself.

As Winston returned to his car, he remembered Mack, a man with no family, found dead right after one such soccer game Helen was apparently cleaning up for. He also remembered an incident involving Helen from the past – an unfortunate mishap where a staff member had accidentally ingested a cleaning supply.

"Interesting," Winston muttered to himself, starting his car. "Very interesting indeed."

This was going to be a long case.

Winston idly flicked through the passport he had received from a fellow officer, who found it thrown aside at the soccer field, where teenagers often conjugated. "Maria," he read aloud from the passport photo. He flipped it over to find another stamp from Denmark and a passport photo stapled to the back – "Chloe, Denmark." Holy hell, what a lead.

Turning his attention to the crime scene, it wasn't long before Detective Winston found himself on the doorstep of Danielle, the local spiritual guru, alternatively known as Maria and Chloe in her past.

Danielle's reputation preceded her not just for her aliases but also for her meticulous cleaning which she considered a spiritual activity. "It's a form of meditation for me, I find serenity in cleanliness," Danielle replied to Winston's gentle ribbing, with a slight smile.

"Is that why you’re against Mack's wedding?" Winston asked. She blinked at him. "Rumor has it, you've taken quite the interest in Mack's so called love-life." 

Danielle, in her belief of spiritual purity, confessed, "Harmful karmic consequences often ensue when one person pledges themselves to someone they do not love. Mack was about to please his parents by making such a mistake, marrying a woman he didn't care for. I wanted Mack to remain single, as I believe it would have maintained his spiritual purity."

She paused to siphon some tea from a kettle, her eyes never leaving Winston. "By the way, Detective, I think you’ve dropped something," she said, pointing at the passport Winston had forgotten in his jacket pocket. "Oh, that?" he asked nonchalantly, "It's your passport, isn’t it? Maria, Chloe, all your aliases, found at the crime scene."

Danielle gave it a fleeting glance and said, "Ah I see, Detective. Still, it's not the one I use currently... I don't need a passport to travel. I have lived in many places under many names, including Sophie in France."

Winston kicked a stone down the road as he left Danielle's residence, pondering on her confessions. "Sophie, France", he mumbled to himself. More identities. More questions. 

Back at the station, he poured over the evidence once more which also had multiples items linking Danielle to the alias Sophie in France. Mack was about to wed a woman he didn’t love just to please his parents... and there he lay on the soccer field, with the smell of bleach fresh in his throat. The same bleach that Mack’s spiritual guru, Maria, Chloe, Sophie, Danielle would stock in volumes almost crazy enough to put a cleaning supply store out of business.

What a case.
